title: Protect nonproduction environments with real access control
statement: Staging, preview, and demonstration environments require authentication at the network or application layer, rather than relying on an unlisted hostname or a crawl directive to keep them private.
rationale: A directive asks well-behaved clients not to index a host, which is not the same as preventing anyone from reading it, and hostnames become public through certificate logs and referrer headers without anyone publishing them.
implementation: Put the environment behind an authentication check that runs before any content is served, and keep the crawl directive as a second layer rather than the only one. An environment already exposed needs its indexed URLs removed as well as the access closed.

verification.method: Request a nonproduction host anonymously and confirm the response is an authentication challenge rather than content, independently of any crawl directive present.

caution: The cited documentation is explicit that a crawl directive is not an access control mechanism, which is the basis for requiring authentication here rather than treating the directive as sufficient.

title: Keep preview URLs unguessable and excluded from indexing
statement: A URL that exposes unpublished content contains a high-entropy token, expires, and carries a directive suppressing indexing, so possession of the link is the only way to reach it and holding it does not make the content public.
rationale: Preview links are shared by email and chat where they leak into referrer headers and link previews, so a guessable or permanent preview URL publishes the draft it was meant to circulate privately.
implementation: Generate the token from a cryptographic source, record an expiry the server enforces, and emit the suppression directive on every preview response. Do not derive the token from the content identifier or a timestamp.

verification.method: Request a preview URL after its expiry and request a sequential variant of its token, recording the status and the indexing directive returned in each case.

title: Keep consent state out of crawler access decisions
statement: Primary content is served to a client that has expressed no consent preference, and the consent mechanism governs optional measurement and personalisation rather than whether the content renders.
rationale: A crawler holds no cookies and answers no dialog, so a page that waits for a consent decision before rendering its content serves an empty page to every client that cannot make one.
implementation: Render the content first and layer the consent prompt over it, gating only the scripts that require consent. Do not make the content's presence in the document conditional on a stored preference.

verification.method: Fetch each route with no cookies and no interaction and confirm the primary content is present in the response body.

caution: The cited page documents that the crawler generally declines cookies, which is the fact this control rests on. The rule that content must not be gated on consent state follows from that fact rather than being stated in the documentation, so this record is tier B.

title: Return neutral metadata on unauthorized responses
statement: A response refusing access carries a title, description, and preview metadata that describe the refusal rather than the protected resource, and reveals nothing about whether that resource exists.
rationale: Metadata describing the protected page turns a refusal into a disclosure, because the title alone can confirm the existence and subject of something the requester was not permitted to see.
implementation: Render the refusal from its own template with fixed metadata, rather than reusing the target page's layout with the content removed. Where existence itself is sensitive, return the same response for a missing and a forbidden resource.

verification.method: Request protected resources without credentials and compare the metadata in the refusal against the metadata the authorized response carries.

title: Isolate tenant content by host and cache key
statement: In a deployment serving several customers from shared infrastructure, whatever distinguishes one tenant from another participates in the cache key at every layer, so a stored response for one tenant can never satisfy a request from another.
rationale: When the distinguishing input is not part of the key, the cache treats two tenants' requests as the same request, and the first response stored is returned to the second tenant as though it were their own.
implementation: Prefer a distinct hostname or path segment per tenant so the key differs naturally, and where a header determines the tenant, name it in the variance declaration and confirm the edge honours it. Never resolve the tenant from a value the cache does not see.

verification.method: Request the same path as two tenants in sequence through the shared cache and confirm each response contains only its own tenant's content.

sources.title: RFC 9111: HTTP Caching, constructing responses from caches

title: Remove erased content from every surface the site controls
statement: When content is deleted for privacy reasons, the route stops serving it with an appropriate status, its sitemap entry is withdrawn, cached copies at the edge are purged, and any structured data or feed that referenced it is regenerated.
rationale: Deleting the record while the URL, the sitemap entry, the cached copy, and the feed all still carry the content means it remains published everywhere except the database.
implementation: Make deletion a single operation that removes the record, purges the edge, regenerates the sitemap and any feed, and sets the route to return the correct status. Verify each of those effects rather than assuming the deletion propagated.

verification.method: Delete a test record and then request its route, its sitemap, its feed, and its cached copy, confirming none of them still returns the content.

caution: This record covers only the surfaces the site itself controls. Removal from third-party caches and search indexes uses separate platform mechanisms, and legal obligations around erasure are outside the scope of this registry.
